title: How to integrate ERP and CRM so data enters once instead of twice
content_html:
Your operations team enters a customer order into the ERP. Your sales team enters the same customer into the CRM. Finance needs the customer details in the accounting system. Three places, three manual entries, three chances to type it wrong. An integrated ERP and CRM stops the retyping and keeps both systems in step.

But integrating ERP and CRM is not a simple checkbox. The systems speak different languages. Fields do not always match. Someone has to decide which system owns the truth when data conflicts. And once the integration runs, something has to watch it and fix it when it breaks.

Here are your real options, what each one costs you, and when each one makes sense.

Built-in connectors: fast if they exist, limited if they don't

Many ERP and CRM vendors ship their own connectors. SAP has connectors to Salesforce. Microsoft Dynamics links to Microsoft 365. If your two systems have an official connector, it is usually the quickest way to start. Setup is faster because the vendor has already mapped the common fields. The connector runs on the vendor's infrastructure, so you do not need to host it yourself.

The catch is scope. Built-in connectors handle the most common workflows. If you need to sync a custom field, apply a business rule, or handle an edge case, the connector often cannot do it. You are stuck with what the vendor chose to connect. Many teams find they outgrow the connector within months.

Integration platforms: flexible for many workflows, fragile at the edges

Zapier, Make and Workato let you build two-way syncs without code. You map fields, set triggers, and the platform handles the sync. These tools are strong when your workflow is standard: "when a deal closes in the CRM, create an order in the ERP" or "when an invoice is paid in the ERP, update the CRM contact record."

Integration platforms shine because they handle many connectors. You can build a sync that touches dozens of systems at once. They also let you add logic: if a field is empty, use a default value; if a customer already exists, update instead of duplicate.

The limits appear when your rules get specific. What happens if two customers have the same name? Which system decides the customer ID? If the ERP rejects an order because stock is zero, does the CRM know that? Integration platforms can handle these cases, but the flows become complex, the rules pile up, and monitoring becomes harder. When a sync fails halfway through, you often have to fix it by hand or rebuild the flow.

Custom integration: built for your exact rules, needs someone to run it

A custom integration is code written to connect your two systems exactly as you need. It can read a customer from the CRM, check for duplicates in the ERP using your own logic, apply your business rules, and sync back the result. Custom integrations do not have the limits of platforms because they are written for your workflow.

The tradeoff is maintenance. Code needs to run somewhere. It needs to be monitored. When the ERP or CRM releases an update, the integration may need changes. If the integration fails, someone has to investigate and fix it. You also need to decide upfront: does the ERP own customer data, or the CRM? What happens if both systems change the same field at the same time? These questions matter more in custom code because you have to answer them explicitly.

What breaks in most integrations

Field mapping is the first problem. The ERP calls it "Customer Code." The CRM calls it "Account ID." The integration has to know they are the same thing. If the mapping is wrong, you create duplicates or lose data.

Duplicate records are the second. If the integration cannot tell whether a customer already exists, it creates a new record every time. Cleaning up duplicates takes hours.

The third is deciding which system is the source of truth. If a customer's address changes in the CRM, should it overwrite the ERP? If the ERP has it marked as inactive, should the CRM respect that? These rules have to be set before the integration runs, and they have to be enforced every time.

When to choose each option

Start with the built-in connector if your systems offer one and your workflow is standard. You get up and running fast with no code and no hosting headaches.

Move to an integration platform like Make or Zapier if you need more logic than the connector offers but your rules are not too complex. These platforms are reliable for common workflows and you pay only for what you use.

Build a custom integration if your workflow is specific to your business, the rules are complex, or you need to sync many fields and handle edge cases. A custom integration costs more upfront but gives you exactly what you need and the flexibility to change it as your business grows. Why Standard Project Controls Software SaaS Misses the Mark for Growing Teams covers the same problem in a different context: off-the-shelf tools often do not fit the way real teams work.

Remember that integrations are not one-time work. Someone has to monitor them, fix broken syncs, and update them when systems change. If you build or buy an integration, plan for ongoing support from day one.
